title: IP Addressing
summary: Public and private IPv4 ranges, APIPA, address classes A to E, choosing a private range, IPv6 basics and address types, tunneling and dual stack, SLAAC, EUI-64, and the chapter written labs.

items: Domain 1.0 Networking concepts: use appropriate IPv4 network addressing (public vs. private, APIPA, RFC 1918, loopback/localhost, subnetting with VLSM and CIDR, and address classes A to E).
Domain 1.0 Networking concepts: evolving use cases, including IPv6 addressing, mitigating address exhaustion, and compatibility requirements (tunneling, dual stack, NAT64).
Domain 3.0 Network operations: implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services, including stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC).

sections.title: Public, private, APIPA, and loopback addresses

items: Public addresses are routable on the Internet. Private addresses (RFC 1918) are not.
Class A private range: 10.0.0.0 through 10.255.255.255.
Class B private range: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255.
Class C private range: 192.168.0.0 through 192.168.255.255.

APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) range: 169.254.0.1 through 169.254.255.254. A client that cannot reach a DHCP server configures itself with an APIPA address and the default Class B mask 255.255.0.0.
Loopback (localhost) addresses point a host at itself. 127.0.0.1 is the one you use.

blocks.text: Seeing 169.254.x.x on a client means DHCP did not answer. It is a symptom to troubleshoot, not an address to keep.

items: The gap between 126 and 128 is the 127 loopback network.
Class D and E have no network and host split because they are not used for ordinary host addressing.

sections.title: Which private range should you use?

items: For a corporate network of any size, consultants use a Class A private network (10.0.0.0) because it gives the most flexibility and room to grow.
Example: Acme Corporation has 14 departments with about 70 users each. A plan of 10.1.x.0 with a /24 mask, where x is the department's subnet number, is easy to design, install, and troubleshoot.
Using 10.0.0.0 with a /24 mask gives 65,536 networks of 254 hosts each.
For a home network, use a Class C private address. It is the easiest to understand and configure, and the default Class C mask gives one network with 254 hosts.

CIDR and VLSM let you give each department or building only the number of addresses it needs, without wasting space. Chapter 8 covers the subnet math. A /24 means 24 of the 32 mask bits are turned on.

sections.title: Why IPv6, and how it differs

items: Without IPv6 the world would run out of IPv4 addresses. IPv6 mitigates address exhaustion.
An IPv6 address is 128 bits long and written in hexadecimal. An IPv4 address is 32 bits long and written in decimal.
If the acronym IP is used alone, it means IPv4.
Link-local addresses are like IPv4 APIPA addresses, but they cannot be routed at all, not even inside your organization.
Unique local addresses are like IPv4 private addresses. They cannot be routed to the Internet, but unlike link-local they can be routed inside your organization.

blocks.text: Link-local: never routed. Unique local: routed inside the organization, never on the Internet.

rows: One-to-one: a packet goes to a single interface
An address assigned to one interface
Used just like a regular public, routable IPv4 address
Always starts with FE80::/10. Not meant to be routed
Starts with FC00::/7. Not routed to the Internet but still globally unique. Used to be called site-local
One-to-nearest: identifies multiple interfaces, delivered only to the first one it finds

items: IPv6 has 128-bit addresses against 32-bit IPv4 addresses, so 96 more bits.
Benefits over IPv4 include more available addresses, a simpler header, and options for authentication and other security.
A MAC address is a 48-bit (6-byte) address physically assigned to a network interface such as a NIC. It is also called a hardware address or a burned-in address.

blocks.text: Match the phrase to the type: single interface is unicast, public-like is global unicast, not routed is link-local, not on the Internet but globally unique is unique local, multiple interfaces is multicast, nearest is anycast.

sections.title: IPv6 compatibility: tunneling, dual stack, NAT64

items: Tunneling carries IPv6 traffic inside IPv4 so it can cross an IPv4-only part of the network.
Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side on the same devices.
NAT64 translates between IPv6 and IPv4 so IPv6-only hosts can reach IPv4 services.
Hosts can use stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) to obtain an IPv6 address without a DHCP server. One way to build the interface ID is EUI-64.
EUI-64 takes the host's 48-bit MAC address and inserts FF:FE in the middle, which makes a 64-bit interface ID.
It also inverts the 7th bit of the first byte, typically changing it from 0 to 1.

rows: Invert the 7th bit of the first byte (00 becomes 02)

blocks.text: Reading an EUI-64 address backwards: drop the FF:FE and flip the 7th bit back to recover the MAC address.

items: Class A is 1 to 126 (8 network bits, 24 host bits). Class B is 128 to 191 (16/16). Class C is 192 to 223 (24/8).
IPv6 exists because IPv4 addresses would run out. It is 128 bits, hexadecimal.
Link-local cannot be routed at all. Unique local can be routed inside the organization.
Read an EUI-64 address: FF:FE is inserted in the middle of the MAC address and the 7th bit of the first byte is inverted.

IPv6 types: unicast is one-to-one, multicast is one-to-many, anycast is one-to-nearest. Global unicast is the public-style address, link-local starts with FE80::/10, unique local starts with FC00::/7, and loopback is ::1.
The 127.0.0.1 loopback is for diagnostics. The whole 127.0.0.1 through 127.255.255.254 range is loopback.

title: IP Subnetting, Troubleshooting IP, and NAT
summary: Why you subnet, default masks and CIDR, the big five subnetting questions, worked /25 example, Class C mask table, classful vs classless and VLSM, the /30 WAN mask, and an introduction to NAT and PAT.

items: Domain 1.0 Networking Concepts, 1.4: explain common networking ports, protocols, services, and traffic types. Traffic types are unicast, multicast, anycast, and broadcast.

Domain 1.0 Networking Concepts, 1.7: use appropriate IPv4 network addressing. This covers public vs. private (APIPA, RFC 1918, loopback/localhost), subnetting (VLSM and CIDR), and IPv4 address classes A to E.
Domain 2.0 Network Implementation, 2.1: explain characteristics of routing technologies, including address translation with NAT and port address translation (PAT).
Add a router to a physical network and you have an internetwork. The hosts on it must now have a logical network addressing scheme to communicate.
IPv6 could be used, but IPv4 is still the most popular, and it is what this chapter covers.
The key to understanding subnetting is understanding the very reason you need to do it. Subnetting splits one network into smaller networks, so each segment on a router gets its own network ID.

sections.title: Default subnet masks and CIDR notation

items: CIDR notation writes how many bits of the mask are turned on, after a slash. 255.255.255.0 has 24 bits on, so it is /24.
The network ID is the part of the address covered by the mask. The host ID is the rest.
1. How many subnets? 2 to the power of the number of subnet bits (mask bits turned on in the interesting octet). For 255.255.255.128 that is 1 bit, so 2^1 = 2.

2. How many hosts per subnet? 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. For /25 there are 7 host bits, so 2^7 - 2 = 126. The 2 removed are the subnet address (all host bits off) and the broadcast address (all host bits on).
3. What are the valid subnets? Block size = 256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet. 256 - 128 = 128. Start at zero and count in the block size: 0, 128.
4. What is the broadcast address of each subnet? The number right before the next subnet, with all host bits turned on. The next subnet after 0 is 128, so the broadcast of the 0 subnet ends in 127.
5. What are the valid hosts? The numbers between the subnet address and its broadcast address.

blocks.text: Write the subnet address and the broadcast address first. The valid hosts are then obvious: everything in between.
Network address 192.168.10.0 with subnet mask 255.255.255.128 (/25). The number 128 is 10000000 in binary, so 1 bit is used for subnetting and 7 bits are left for hosts.
/25 on a Class C gives 2 subnets with 126 hosts each. Subnets: 0 and 128. Broadcasts: 127 and 255.

sections.title: Class C masks at a glance

blocks.text: The same five steps work for every Class C mask. Compare each row with the /25 example.
Quick check: subnets times block size always equals 256 in a Class C network.

items: A classful network uses the same subnet mask on every host and router interface.
Classless routing lets you use different size masks in the same network. Giving each link a mask that fits its need is called variable length subnet masking (VLSM).
CIDR (classless inter-domain routing) is the slash notation used to write those masks, such as /25 or /30.

sections.title: Real world: the /30 mask for WAN links

items: Scenario: you administer Acme Corporation in San Francisco with dozens of WAN links to the corporate office. Every host and router interface uses the same mask, and you must pick a mask for point-to-point links.
A /24 (255.255.255.0) gives each WAN network 254 hosts, but a WAN link uses only 2 addresses. That wastes 252 addresses per link.
A /30 (255.255.255.252) leaves 2 host bits, so 2^2 - 2 = 2 hosts per subnet. That is exactly enough for the two ends of a link, and no precious addresses are wasted.

blocks.text: Point-to-point WAN links: use 255.255.255.252 (/30). Two usable hosts, nothing wasted.

items: Network address translation (NAT) is introduced at the end of the chapter, with the difference between static NAT, dynamic NAT, and NAT overloading, which is port address translation (PAT).
Static NAT: a fixed one-to-one mapping between an inside address and a public address.
Dynamic NAT: inside addresses are mapped to public addresses taken from a pool as they are needed.
NAT overloading (PAT): many inside hosts share a single public address, and the translating device tells their conversations apart by port number.

blocks.text: NAT overloading and PAT are the same thing. The chapter lists both names, and the exam objectives use PAT.

Answer the big five for any mask: subnets, hosts per subnet, valid subnets, broadcast of each, valid hosts.
Hosts per subnet is 2^h - 2. Block size is 256 minus the interesting octet.
Use /30 (255.255.255.252) for point-to-point WAN links.
Be able to find valid IP addresses and subnet masks by reading a network diagram.
Know the difference between static NAT, dynamic NAT, and NAT overloading (PAT).

title: Routing Protocols
summary: Distance-vector, link-state, hybrid, and path-vector protocols; administrative distance; metrics; RIP versions; loops; and static vs dynamic routing.

rows: Passes its routing table to neighbors. No full topology map.
Learns every link and builds the same topology map, then runs Dijkstra.
Routes between autonomous systems, tracking the AS path.

blocks.text: RIP has no topology table. It only trusts what its neighbors tell it.
AD ranks how much the router trusts each route source. When two sources offer the same route, the lowest AD is installed. Metrics only break ties between routes from the same protocol.

items: When a router receives two updates for the same remote network, AD is the first thing it checks. The route with the lower AD goes into the routing table.
Internal EIGRP routes carry AD 90. External EIGRP routes, redistributed into EIGRP from another source, carry AD 170.
AD 255 means the source is unknown. The router never uses a route with AD 255.

blocks.text: A static default route (AD 1) beats a RIP default route (AD 120), even if RIP has a lower metric.
Real world: a wise network engineer does not change the default administrative distance values for protocols. Leave AD at its defaults so every router makes the same, predictable choice.

sections.title: Real world: watching the network with SNMP traps

blocks.text: Leaving AD alone does not mean ignoring routing. A senior engineer managed his team of network engineers with SNMP traps, so problems reached them as they happened. An SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) trap is an unsolicited, real-time alert that an SNMP-enabled device (the agent) sends to a central network management system (NMS) to report a critical event or status change, without waiting to be polled.

items: Transport: traps use UDP port 162. Polling, such as GET requests, uses UDP port 161.
Unsolicited alerts: devices push a message only when a trigger happens, which cuts the overhead of constant polling.
OID (Object Identifier): a dotted-decimal string that uniquely identifies the event or object.
Varbinds (variable bindings): key-value pairs with context, such as sysUpTime, snmpTrapOID, interface indexes, or error descriptions.
Timestamp and agent address: when the event happened and which device sent it.

rows: linkDown or linkUp when a physical or logical interface flaps
Power supply loss, fan failure, high temperature, memory exhaustion
Authentication failures, wrong community string attempts, firewall security triggers
BGP session drops, EGP neighbor loss
No. Fire and forget; the agent never knows if the NMS got it.
Yes. The NMS must send an acknowledgment.
The agent retries until it gets an ACK.

items: Upgrade to SNMPv3. SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c send community strings (public, private) in clear text; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption.
Compile MIBs on the NMS. Load the vendor MIBs (for example Cisco or Juniper) into the management platform, such as PRTG, LogicMonitor, or Netdata, so raw OIDs show as readable text.
Rate-limit and filter. Prevent trap storms during a major outage by filtering redundant or low-priority traps, and pair traps with periodic polling for complete visibility.
Use Cisco EEM (Embedded Event Manager) to script custom triggers that turn CLI events or log messages into tailored SNMP notifications.

blocks.text: Exam memory hook: traps go to UDP 162, polls go to UDP 161. A trap is not acknowledged; an INFORM is. For more, see Cisco's SNMP trap configuration guide or LogicMonitor's SNMP trap overview.

items: RIP uses hop count. 1 to 15 is usable, and 16 or more is unreachable.
OSPF uses cost: reference bandwidth (100 Mbps) divided by interface bandwidth. Faster links cost less.
EIGRP uses a composite metric of delay, bandwidth, reliability, and load, weighted by K values.

blocks.text: RIPv2 multicasts. It does not broadcast.
A routing loop sends packets around a set of routers without ever reaching the destination. Each hop lowers the TTL, and the packet is dropped when TTL reaches 0.
TTL expiry on its own does not prove a routing loop; it can also mean the destination is too many hops away. The loop itself is packets circulating between routers and never arriving.
Split horizon is a loop-prevention rule used by distance-vector protocols such as RIP and IGRP. A router does not advertise a route back out the interface it learned that route on.

items: Example: Router B learns 10.0.0.0 from Router A on its link to A. B does not send that route back to A on that link.
B still advertises the route out its other interfaces.
Without split horizon, A and B can pass the same route back and forth, and the packets loop.

blocks.text: Split horizon blocks one route on one interface. It does not stop every update, and it does not stop broadcast storms on switches.

items: Dynamic routing reroutes around failures with no administrator action.
Static routing is typed in by an administrator and stays until someone changes it.
Default routes also need an administrator to change them if they fail.
Dynamic routing costs more RAM, CPU, and bandwidth, but it gives resiliency.
NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) discovers neighboring devices on IPv6 networks.
Router advertisements (RA) announce the gateway so hosts can find it.
Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.
Tunneling carries IPv6 inside IPv4. Teredo and ISATAP are tunneling methods.

title: Switching and Virtual LANs
summary: Switch learning and forwarding, VLANs, access and trunk ports, 802.1Q tagging, Spanning Tree, port security, QoS, and PoE.

items: Switches give the lowest latency and highest bandwidth. They use ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits) to forward frames in hardware.
A hub is a multiport repeater. It sends every signal to every port and shares the bandwidth.
A bridge is a software-based switch with higher latency than a switch.
Routers add latency because each packet is decapsulated, routed, and re-encapsulated.

sections.title: How a switch learns and forwards

items: A switch learns MAC addresses from the source MAC address of incoming frames, and stores them in its MAC address table.
It forwards each frame based on the destination MAC address in the table.
If the destination MAC address is not in the table, the switch floods the frame to all ports in the same VLAN.
Broadcast frames stay inside the VLAN they start in, because they cannot cross a router.

blocks.text: Switches learn from the source MAC address, not the destination. The destination decides where the frame goes.

items: Adding a VLAN increases the number of broadcast domains. It also increases the number of collision domains.
All switch ports start in VLAN 1 from the factory. VLANs 1 and 1002 to 1005 are protected by IOS and cannot be deleted.
Static VLANs are configured manually on each port. The node does not know which VLAN it is in.
Dynamic VLANs assign a port based on the device's MAC address, using a VMPS (VLAN Membership Policy Server). They are deprecated, and 802.1X is the recommended replacement.
Converting a flat layer 2 network to routed VLANs makes design more flexible but adds complexity to operations.

rows: One VLAN for an end device
VLAN tag removed before the frame leaves the port
Multiple VLANs between switches or routers
Voice traffic on an access port
Tags only when the CoS value is changed from the default

items: Hosts usually connect to access links.
Native VLAN traffic is untagged on the trunk. It is often used for management traffic between switches before both sides are configured as trunks.
Port security should be set on an access port. A trunk carries many MAC addresses, so port security does not work well there.
802.1Q is the open-standard trunking protocol. ISL is Cisco-only, so it cannot be used between switches from different vendors.
802.1Q inserts a 4-byte (32-bit) tag between the source MAC address and the type field.
The tag holds a 16-bit TPID of 0x8100, a 3-bit CoS field, a 1-bit drop-eligible indicator, and a 12-bit VLAN ID.

blocks.text: Tagged traffic is not placed on the native VLAN. Only untagged traffic is.

items: STP (802.1D) prevents loops in switched networks. RSTP (802.1w) is the faster version.
The root bridge is the switch with the lowest priority. If every priority is at the default, the lowest MAC address wins.
The default state for an STP port is blocking.
It takes 50 seconds for STP to converge from blocking to forwarding.
A routed, VLAN-enabled network is more flexible for user management and design than a flat layer 2 network, although operations get more complex.
To segment a workgroup such as R&D, create a new VLAN, configure a routed SVI (switched virtual interface), and apply ACLs to the VLAN interface.
ACLs belong on the VLAN (layer 3) interface. Extended ACLs cannot be applied to layer 2 switch ports.
Placing a new server in the new VLAN, or trunking the file server to both VLANs, does not restrict access.

blocks.text: Port security limits a switch port to a set number of MAC addresses. The addresses can be configured in advance or learned dynamically. It is set on an access port in access mode. It does not use jumbo frames or 802.1X, which control frame size and user authentication instead.

items: CoS is the layer 2 QoS method. It is a 3-bit field in the 802.1Q tag that maps to eight queues.
ToS and DiffServ are layer 3 QoS methods.
802.3at delivers 25.5 watts of power over Ethernet (PoE).

blocks.text: VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol) propagates the VLAN database from a master copy on a server switch to client switches. It does not negotiate trunks or handle trunk encapsulation.

title: Introduction to IP Routing
summary: The IP routing process, frames versus packets, MAC addresses and ARP, reading a route table, static and dynamic routing, autonomous systems, and route selection.

items: A router decides where to send a packet using its route table and the destination network of the packet. It does not need the destination host, the originating network, or the return path to route the packet.
Routers rebuild Ethernet frames at routed hops. Without NAT, source and destination IP addresses stay the same; TTL decreases and the IPv4 header checksum changes.
A frame carries a packet to only two places: a host on the local network, or a router interface when the packet is going to a remote network.
When the destination is on another network, the host sets the destination MAC address to the default gateway. The destination IP address never changes.

blocks.text: Ethernet frames are local and rebuilt at routed hops. Without NAT, the IP source and destination remain end to end, while routers update TTL and the IPv4 header checksum.

items: MAC (hardware) addresses are always local. They are used only on the local LAN and never pass a router interface.
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) finds the MAC address of the default gateway, or of a local host, from an IP address.
A host ARPs for the destination if it is on the same network. If not, it ARPs for the default gateway.
At the far end, the router interface facing the destination network ARPs for the destination host.
Reverse ARP (RARP) does the opposite, deriving an IP address from a MAC address, similar to DHCP. It does not update route tables.

rows: View the ARP cache on a Windows or Mac host
View the ARP cache on a Cisco router or switch
View the route table on a Cisco router

blocks.text: The chapter text prints arp -g in Exercise 9.1 and in question 6, but the command on a host is arp -a (question 18). Cisco routers use show ip arp.

items: The route table is the router's map of the internetwork. Routing decisions are made by destination network, not by host.
A C in the table means the network is directly connected because it is configured on an interface. An S is a static route.
The gateway of last resort is the default route. If it is not set and no route matches, the packet is dropped.
To find the exit interface, match the destination IP address to the network that contains it. 172.16.20.94 falls inside 172.16.20.64/27, so the exit interface is FastEthernet 0/2 (question 14).

blocks.text: A router with these four routes has no match for 172.16.20.100. That address sits between the /27 blocks, so the packet is dropped.

rows: The next device on this local network. For a remote destination, the default gateway.
The sender on this local network. Rewritten at every router hop.
Identifies the protocol inside the frame. 0x0800 is IPv4 and 0x0806 is ARP.
The IP packet. Without NAT its IP endpoints stay the same; routers change TTL and the IPv4 header checksum.
A 4-byte cyclic redundancy check at the end of the frame. The destination uses it to verify the frame arrived intact.

blocks.text: The source MAC, destination MAC, and EtherType are included when the FCS is calculated, but only the FCS tells the receiver that the frame is intact.

items: If the router has no route to the destination network, it drops the packet.
The router also sends an ICMP destination unreachable message to the sender. The original packet is never returned.
Logging happens only if it is configured. Routers do not ask for dynamic updates when they meet an unknown network.
If a ping is lost along the way, the sender sees Request timed out. Destination unreachable appears when a router lacks the route.

items: The main job of a routing protocol is to update routing tables.
Convergence is the term for the result of all routes being updated in the routing table through a dynamic routing protocol. Faster convergence is better.

blocks.text: If a question asks for routing that is automated as new locations are added, the answer is dynamic routing, not static routing, DHCP, or RARP.

items: An autonomous system (AS) is a collection of networks or subnets in the same administrative domain.
An interior gateway protocol (IGP) is a dynamic routing protocol used inside an autonomous system. RIP, EIGRP, and OSPF are IGPs.
An exterior gateway protocol (EGP) is a dynamic routing protocol used between autonomous systems. BGP is the EGP in use today.
Administrative distance (AD) decides the most trusted route when two or more routes to the same network exist.
Distance-vector and link-state describe how routing protocols share and calculate routes. Chapter 10 covers them in detail.
Exam objective 2.1 lists three factors for route selection: prefix length, administrative distance, and metric.
A router first prefers the route with the longest matching prefix, because it is the most specific.
If prefix lengths tie, the router prefers the lowest administrative distance.
If administrative distance also ties, the router prefers the lowest metric.
